📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The ocean has an extraordinary ability to transform how we feel. Its rhythms slow us down. Its vastness helps us gain perspective. Its beauty invites us to pause. Its resilience inspires hope.

And this impact may actually be backed by science. It’s called the Blue Mind Theory. Essentially, research has revealed a link between time spent near water, especially on the coast, and both better well-being and lower distress.

That’s why Calm has partnered with Blue Planet III from BBC Studios, encouraging you to take a mindful moment to release stress, experience awe, and escape beneath the waves, wherever you are. Together, we’ve created a latest collection of content that spotlights the soothing sounds and stunning sights of the deep blue sea.

Twenty-five years after the groundbreaking original series first brought the ocean into homes around the world, the fresh Blue Planet III illuminates incredible new stories from some of Earth's most key and least understood environments.

And now, the most calming elements of the series are being reimagined in the context of Calm.

Here are the highlights of the collection:.

💙 Dive into Blue Planet III — a new immersive soundscape that takes you on a rhythmic journey through tropical seas alive with dolphins, the boundless open ocean, and finally seasonal seas that feature the mating calls of southern right whales.

💙 Drift Through the Reef — a mesmerizing, meditative montage of colorful coral.

💙 Find Your Flow — a delightful dance between sea lions and a massive bait ball, a school of thousands of small fish all swimming in unison.

💙 Bask in the Blue  — an entrancing visualscape of a seahorse floating through glistening sunbeams.

💙 The Sound of Blue Planet III — the series’ enchanting theme song, from Hans Zimmer, Thom Lukas & Laurentia Editha for Bleeding Fingers Music.

So dive in (pun intended) to the mindful magic of the ocean and find out where to watch Blue Planet III from BBC Studios.

Industry observers note that mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

The most widely cited framework for income classes comes from the Pew Research Center, which uses a straightforward formula based on the national median household income. Pew defines three tiers:.

Using the most recent Census Bureau data with a national median household income of approximately $84,900, the thresholds for a three-person household look like this:.

Sources indicate that the "upper middle class" label is not an official Pew category — it is a colloquial term most commonly used to describe the band between the middle of the middle class and the beginning of the upper class. Think of it as the top quarter of the middle-income range through the entry point of the upper-income range: households earning roughly $106,000 to $169,800.

These definitions are adjusted for household size using an equivalence scale. A single person needs less income than a family of five to achieve the same standard of living. Pew adjusts all income figures to a three-person household equivalent, which is why the thresholds you see in different sources sometimes vary — they may be using different household sizes as their reference point.

Recent findings suggest that national income thresholds are useful starting points, but they obscure a critical reality: the cost of living varies so dramatically across the United States that the same income places you in different classes depending on where you live. Pew Research's cost-of-living adjusted data reveals just how stark these differences are.

Sources indicate that A household earning $150,000 in Jackson, Mississippi — where the cost of living is roughly 83% of the national average — has purchasing power equivalent to about $180,700 nationally. That same $150,000 in San Francisco, where costs run about 180% of the national average, has purchasing power equivalent to only $83,300 — technically middle class by Pew's national definitions.

In a recent development, this explains why so many households earning $150,000 to $200,000 in coastal cities feel middle class despite technically being upper-income by national standards. They are not wrong — their lived experience of housing costs, childcare, and taxes genuinely consumes their income at the same rate as middle-income households in lower-cost areas.

According to recent reports, income class and wealth class are not the same thing. The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances reveals that high income does not automatically translate to high net worth. Many upper-income households carry large mortgages, student loans, and car payments that consume much of their earnings. Meanwhile, some middle-income households with high savings rates accumulate substantial wealth over time.

It has been revealed that the FI community lives in this gap. A household earning $90,000 that saves 50% of their income and invests consistently will have a higher net worth within 10-15 years than a household earning $250,000 that saves 5%. Income determines your ceiling; savings rate determines your trajectory. This is why ChooseFI focuses on savings rate and investable net worth as the primary metrics of financial progress — not income class labels.

According to recent reports, the financial independence community occupies a unique position in the income class framework. Survey data from FIRE-focused communities suggests the median household income among FI seekers is roughly $130,000 to $160,000 — placing most in the upper-middle-class to lower-upper-income range. However, successful FI stories span the entire income spectrum, from teachers earning $55,000 to tech executives earning $500,000.

What distinguishes FI community members from their income peers is not what they earn but what they keep. While the average upper-middle-class household saves 8-12% of income, FI-path households in the same income range typically save 40-60%. This results in net worth accumulation that dramatically outpaces their income class peers.

The lesson from this comparison is that income class labels describe your earning power, but they say nothing about your financial trajectory. A middle-income household on the FI path will typically surpass the net worth of upper-income households who spend freely. The FI framework redefines "class" around financial freedom rather than consumption — your class is determined not by what you can afford to buy, but by how many years of expenses your investments can cover.

Income class definitions use household income, which combines the earnings of all adults in a home. This creates a nuance worth understanding: a dual-income household where each partner earns $75,000 has the same household income ($150,000) as a single-earner household at that level, but the dual-income household often faces higher total costs (two commutes, potentially more childcare) and different tax treatment. When evaluating where you fall, always use your total household income before taxes and compare to thresholds adjusted for your household size.

In a recent development, the distinction between wealth and income is the foundation of financial independence. Your income class describes your present earning power. Your net worth describes your accumulated financial freedom. The FI community's central insight is that you can move from any income class to financial independence by controlling the gap between what you earn and what you spend — and investing the difference consistently in low-cost index funds over time.

In a recent development, whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class by any definition, your path to financial independence depends on one number: your savings rate. A middle-income household saving 50% of their income will reach FI decades before an upper-income household saving 5%. Focus on growing the gap between what you earn and what you spend — the class label takes care of itself.

Add up all pre-tax income for your household — wages, self-employment, investment income, and any other sources. Compare to the Pew thresholds adjusted for your household size. For a three-person household, middle income is $56,600 to $169,800.

Sources indicate that use a cost-of-living calculator to adjust your income to the national equivalent. A $120,000 income in a city with 130% cost-of-living has the same purchasing power as $92,300 nationally. This adjusted number is a more honest reflection of your class position.

Your net worth — assets minus liabilities — is a better indicator of financial health than income alone. The median net worth for upper-middle-class households is roughly $465,000. If you are above that with a lower income, you are wealthier than your income class suggests.

Divide your annual savings (including employer retirement contributions) by your gross income. The national average is under 5%. The FI community targets 40-60%. Your savings rate is the single most important predictor of when you will reach financial independence.

Multiply your annual spending by 25 to find your FI number (based on the 4% safe withdrawal rate). Then use your current savings rate and existing net worth to estimate how many years until you reach that number. This timeline matters more than any income class label.

According to Pew Research, upper-income households earn more than double the national median household income. For a three-person household in 2026, that threshold is approximately $169,800. However, this varies significantly by location — in San Francisco, you would need roughly $306,000 to have the same purchasing power as $169,800 nationally.

Sources indicate that upper middle class generally describes households in the top 20-30% of earners but below the top 5% — roughly $106,000 to $169,800 for a three-person household. Upper class typically refers to households above $169,800 (top 19%). The top 5% begins at roughly $280,000 and the top 1% at approximately $590,000. These are income-based definitions and do not account for net worth.

Industry observers note that by national standards, $200,000 household income places you in the upper-income category (above the $169,800 threshold for a three-person household). However, in high-cost cities like San Francisco, Fresh York, or Boston, $200,000 has purchasing power equivalent to roughly $111,000 to $130,000 nationally — solidly middle class in terms of lived experience.

The Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances indicates the median net worth of upper-income households is approximately $805,400. The top 10% of U.S. households by net worth have $1.9 million or more, and the top 1% have $11.1 million or more. Net worth is a more meaningful measure of financial security than income because it reflects accumulated wealth, not just current earning power.

Industry observers note that lifestyle inflation is the primary reason. Many households increase their spending in lockstep with income increases — larger homes, newer cars, private schools, premium vacations — leaving little margin for savings. A household earning $300,000 that spends $290,000 accumulates wealth more slowly than one earning $100,000 that spends $50,000. The FI community calls this the HENRY problem: High Earner, Not Rich Yet.

It has been revealed that pew Research adjusts income thresholds using an equivalence scale based on household size. A single person needs roughly $56,600 to be middle income (the lower bound), while a family of five needs roughly $126,500 for the same standard of living. Larger households need more income to achieve the same class designation because they have more people sharing the resources.

Sources indicate that income class labels provide useful context for understanding where you stand relative to other American households, but they are a poor measure of financial health. Plenty of upper-income households are one job loss away from financial crisis because they spend everything they earn, while many middle-income households on the FI path have built net worth that places them in the top 10% of all Americans. The framework that matters most is not whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class — it is whether the gap between your income and your spending is large enough to build financial independence within a timeline that matters to you. Focus on three numbers: your savings rate, your investable net worth, and your FI number. Everything else is a label that describes your present circumstances, not your financial future.

Industry News: How to Make Better Decisions in the Age of AI

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2095 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, artificial intelligence can summarize research, generate ideas, and analyze enormous amounts of data in seconds.
  • Sources indicate that AI has the power to enhance decision-making—or to overwhelm it.
  • According to recent reports, she argues that the rise of AI actually makes certain human qualities like reflection, empathy, values, and moral judgment even more important.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, artificial intelligence can summarize research, generate ideas, and analyze enormous amounts of data in seconds. The power of that little “Ask anything” AI prompt box is immense, but can it help us make wiser decisions? Cheryl Strauss Einhorn, author of The Human Edge: Smarter Decisions in the Age of AI, writes:.

Sources indicate that AI has the power to enhance decision-making—or to overwhelm it. It can illuminate pathways we might not have seen or narrow our choices in ways we do not fully recognize. As AI systems become more integrated into our lives, the challenge is no longer simply about harnessing their power but about leading them with clarity, discernment, and commitment to human agency.

According to recent reports, she argues that the rise of AI actually makes certain human qualities like reflection, empathy, values, and moral judgment even more important. We spoke with her about why human judgment is a competitive advantage, how to engage our values when we prompt AI, and how AI can help us clarify our thinking.

Recent findings suggest that kia Afcari: You argue that AI makes human judgment more, not less, key. How can we make sure that the values of kindness and care are reflected when we use AI to help us make decisions?

Cheryl Strauss Einhorn: AI has no values. It has biases and influences by those who have designed it, and from whatever information has been fed into it. So to be sure that prosocial values are reflected when we use AI, we humans need to bring them into the work that we do together.

It has been revealed that when working with an AI tool, we want to be asking ourselves, What is the problem that I’m solving? Why am I solving it? What is the context? And so we really need to be intentional with AI, because without asking ourselves those things first, AI doesn’t know why we’re coming to it.

Before you actually sit down with a tool, you can muster those values and those crucial factors related to the problem that you’re solving, and then articulate them and communicate them to the machine.

If we let the machine think for us, we can lose that sense of right and wrong, for example, because we actually care about all of those details that AI can’t possibly know about the problems that we’re solving and the people that we’re solving those problems with and for.

For example, you might ask yourself or your AI tool: Before I act, help me think through the people, relationships, and responsibilities this decision affects—not just the outcome it produces.

Industry observers note that this type of human-centric AI interaction helped Felice, a food scientist at a pet food organization, who was responsible for developing new recipes that balance nutrition, taste, and market trends. She often has to delegate tasks within her research team, ensuring that product testing, ingredient sourcing, and regulatory compliance all move forward smoothly. Using AI, she was able to analyze workloads and expertise that suggested the best person for each task, but only Felice understood the deeper dynamics at play—who works best under tight deadlines, who has a passion for innovative formulations, and who needs mentorship. When AI recommended assigning a crucial stability test to her most experienced technician, this prompt supported her thinking about a different option: giving it to the junior scientist who was eager to develop his skills in quality assurance. The AI tool’s choices made sense based on efficiency, but Felice’s decision ensured both short-term success and long-term team development.

Sources indicate that KA: In the book, your “cheetah” metaphor celebrates slowing down. Why is a strategic pause so important when working with AI?

CSE: The cheetah metaphor relates that although this is an animal that goes zero to 60 in about three seconds, its hunting prowess actually comes from being able to decelerate up to nine miles an hour in a single stride. And the reason why that’s so important in problem solving and decision making is that’s where you build agility, flexibility, and maneuverability. Do I want to stay the course, or do I want to pivot and do something else?

Industry observers note that this pause allows you to chunk your learning and pry open that cognitive space for new information and insight. With an AI tool, it’s so notable because there’s a difference between speed and quality.

In a recent development, when something truly matters to us, we want to make sure that we’re solving the problem in a way that solves it holistically, that takes care of the people who are involved in the problem with us. And when we’re moving really quickly, sometimes those very vital factors are hard to bring forward. So there’s a real difference between what is efficient and what is effective.

KA: Why can having more information make it harder—not easier—to make good decisions?

Industry observers note that CSE: Francis Bacon once stated, “Knowledge is power,” but that’s not really true anymore, right? We now have all of the answers with AI to a lot of commonly asked questions and some uncommon questions.

We need to make sure we’re defining the problem that we’re solving, that we are understanding and communicating the motivation and providing the context, because you don’t want all the information. Otherwise, we’re going to end up with analysis paralysis.

According to recent reports, one thing people can use is what I call the “vision of success” question. This question asks you to time travel, to jump over the decision to see that the decision has been made well. What’s happening? What are those few things that if they don’t succeed, the decision fails? It’s actually very powerful, because it allows you to clearly identify so that you can articulate those factors that you absolutely need to be able to share with AI. These become the constraints and boundaries that set the perimeter around the decision, so that it can give you research that’s targeted and focused on those things.

For example, Max deciding where to spend his next vacation. Asking AI for help directly—without turning to himself first—he got a list of destinations, airline options, and local attractions, complete with ratings, reviews, and price comparisons. On paper, that sounds ideal. But in reality, Max promptly found himself paralyzed by the sheer amount of information. What if he picked a less-than-perfect hotel? What if he overlooked a hidden gem? AI has handed him a mountain of data, but it didn’t necessarily make the decision any easier.

However, when he used the “vision of success” question, he was able to realize and to share with his AI tool: “I want to return home feeling genuinely rested, having spent quality time with my family, without overspending or feeling like I missed the experience I was hoping for.”.

It has been revealed that only then does AI have a meaningful problem to solve. Instead of searching for the “best” vacation—a question with no objective answer—it can help Max find the destination most likely to produce the outcome he actually wants. AI can’t define success but it can optimize for the success you define.

KA: How does the AREA method help people make wiser decisions, especially when AI is involved? CSE: AREA is more than an acronym—it’s a framework for challenging our assumptions and thinking mistakes, and actively includes the perspectives of others. It stands for Absolute, Relative, Exploration and Exploitation, and Analysis.

According to recent reports, the first “A,” Absolute, focuses on primary, unfiltered information straight from primary sources. “R,” Relative, shifts to external viewpoints—secondary sources connected to the subject. “E,” Exploration and Exploitation, fuels creativity: Exploration broadens research through interviews and unconventional sources, while Exploitation turns inward, challenging personal biases and assumptions. The final “A,” Analysis, synthesizes everything, bringing clarity and structure to complex decisions.

When using AI, a system like AREA becomes even more crucial because AI doesn’t eliminate bias—it can reflect and sometimes amplify biases in its training data, design, and the way we use it. Good decisions require a process that helps us recognize and challenge both AI’s biases and our own.

In a recent development, for AI, so much of the information, for example, is from Reddit. Information can be incomplete or outdated, and you also know that you’re interacting with a liar. It’s a machine that just gives you answers that are wrong sometimes.

So you need to be able to have a quality due diligence process to not only be able to use the tool effectively, but to be able to evaluate its outcome. Too often, people look at an answer with AI and think that it’s a transaction, and they can just take it. AREA is going to help you make sure that it’s a conversation. So you have an evidence-based perspective that has looked at a variety of stakeholder viewpoints, and made sure that you have pried open that cognitive space to challenge the natural, well-worn mental pathways that we all lean on every day.

KA: How can we use AI in ways that strengthen—rather than undermine—our values and agency?

According to recent reports, CSE: It’s a great question. I think the new competitive advantage is going to be self-awareness.

This is the first tool that actually asks for some of our cognitive load; it wants us to offload some of our decisions to it. And this is a machine fundamentally about decision making, because we ask it for something and it gives us an answer. But there’s a very interesting invitation here, which is to each of us to get to know ourselves better.

It has been revealed that we each have a special sauce, which is the way that we make our decisions, and we make thousands of them every single day. But most of us have not sat down and noted to themselves, What does that process actually look like? Can I actually name those pieces and put language to it?

There is this invitation to get to know our thinking so that we can translate it better, and not only for the tool. How helpful would it be in conversation with our colleagues to be able to say clearly, This is how I’m actually going through the steps, this is how I’m thinking about it, these are the variables that I’m prioritizing, and here’s what I think is the most diagnostic.

According to recent reports, you can think about your thinking skills as muscles. If we turn over our cognitive load, we will also weaken it. But if we actually take this invitation to understand our self-awareness and our metacognition, we can make sure that we strengthen those tools.

AI is a tool that has so many implications for our environment and for our world, in addition to the fact that it has implications for our actual thinking skills.

Industry observers note that so I would say that the invitation is to turn to yourself first. Ask yourself why you’re using the tool, and whether or not you should be turning to yourself instead. And either way, bring your own thinking forward before sitting down, so that you can feel far more comfortable that you can problem-solve both with it and beyond it.

  • Sources indicate that during the presentation titled “Brain Fog or ADHD?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Preliminary evidence shows self-reported brain fog decreases and executive function improves in perimenopausal women treated with ADHD medications.

Industry observers note that stimulant and non-stimulant medications used to treat ADHD significantly improve self-reported executive dysfunction in perimenopausal women without ADHD, according to preliminary evidence presented at the annual meeting of The Menopause Society last month in San Diego. (These findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.)1.

Sources indicate that during the presentation titled “Brain Fog or ADHD? Executive Dysfunction in Perimenopause: A Scoping Review of the Role of ADHD Medications,” researchers discussed the effectiveness of two ADHD medications: lisdexamphetamine (brand name: Vyvanse), a stimulant, and atomoxetine, a non-stimulant. They studied the impact of these medications on cognition and ADHD symptom severity in women aged 45 to 60 years during the perimenopausal period. The systematic review included three crossover randomized controlled trials involving 60 patients and two cross-sectional studies of 6,048 patients from Iceland and the U.K.

It has been revealed that the study found that both lisdexamphetamine (LDX) and atomoxetine (ATX) significantly improve self-reported executive dysfunction, as measured by the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, compared to placebo. The BADDS scores for LDX users dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared to 29.8 with placebo. The BADDS scores for ATX users fell from 38.6 to 25.5, compared to 30.1 with placebo. Neuroimaging data from a subset of women taking LDX further supports these findings.

During perimenopause, declining or fluctuating estrogen levels affect dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex of the brain. As a result, many perimenopausal women experience “brain fog,” which is an umbrella term for forgetfulness, slow thinking, difficulty finding words, and reduced concentration, which can also be a symptom of ADHD. This overlap often leaves clinicians trying to discern whether a patient’s brain fog stems from hormonal fluctuations or undiagnosed ADHD, or both.

“Many women at perimenopause notice changes in focus, memory, and organization that look a lot like ADHD, and the two can be hard to tell apart,” stated lead author Jennifer Tat, M.D. candidate and fourth-year medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Science Center in Memphis.

Recent findings suggest that in an ADDitude survey of more than 5,000 women with diagnosed and undiagnosed ADHD, 94% of survey respondents mentioned their ADHD symptoms grew more severe during perimenopause and menopause. During this stage, respondents said the most impactful ADHD symptoms were brain fog or memory challenges, and overwhelm, both of which 70% of women said had a “life-altering impact” in their 40s and 50s.

“Brain fog became unmanageable,” wrote one 45-year-old mother of two who entered perimenopause at age 41. “Distractibility increased and my inability to complete work tasks in an appropriate amount of time decreased. I began spending all night working just to keep up. Things that I used to have unconscious strategies to deal with were no longer manageable.”.

In a recent development, “I never experienced rage or brain fog before perimenopause,” wrote one woman. “Overwhelm has been more frequent in recent years, and depression began in my 40s. I definitely attribute some of this to hormonal changes.”.

Recent findings suggest that “In perimenopause, the brain fog and memory, inattention, distractibility, perfectionism, hyperactivity, and restlessness issues become progressively worse,” wrote a 52-year-old woman diagnosed with ADHD at age 50. “I have always had these symptoms, but I was able to manage them with systems that I created for myself. My ability to manage them has declined significantly, and this makes these symptoms seem like they are the worst they have ever been.”.

While preliminary evidence from the systematic review found ADHD medications improve subjective executive function, the medications had little to no significant impact on objective cognitive measures, according to tests measuring working memory and sustained attention.

Prior research suggests otherwise.

It has been revealed that in the ADDitude article “Could ADHD Medications Improve Memory, Focus & Organization in Menopausal Women? The Research Says Yes,” the late Thomas E. Brown, Ph.D., described how his research with C. Neill Epperson, M.D., found ADHD medications alleviated cognitive problems resembling ADHD symptoms in menopausal women without ADHD.

According to recent reports, the series of three studies measured symptoms with BADDS, which Brown developed. The first study found that ATX treatment significantly improved BADDS scores for working memory; focus scores improved in BADDS scores for women treated with ATX.2 In the second study, executive functions improved, including an objective measure of short-term working memory, in 41% of menopausal women taking 20 to 60 mg LDX daily, compared to 17% for the women on the placebo.3 The third study examined the effects of LDX on the brain functioning of women with no history of ADHD, but with reported cognitive difficulties with working memory, organization, focus, and attention that had begun during menopause.4.

Sources indicate that “As predicted, neuroimaging data showed that LDX activated executive networks in specific areas of the brain,” Brown wrote. “Those data also showed that LDX’s effect on specific brain regions was associated with improved BADDS scores overall, and with BADDS scores for activation and alertness/effort. Imaging data indicated that improvements in brain activation were significantly larger when women were on LDX than when they were on placebo.”.

The studies were published in peer-reviewed medical journals in 2011, 2015, and 2017; however, Brown wrote in 2021, “results of that research have not yet been widely recognized.”.

Sources indicate that there is right now no FDA-approved pharmacological intervention for executive dysfunction and brain fog during perimenopause or menopause. Research on the most effective treatments for ADHD during perimenopause is limited as well. That remarked, Patricia Quinn, M.D., explained during a 2026 ADDitude webinar that available data and observational evidence suggest that many women could benefit from estrogen supplementation and increased stimulant dosages during this phase.

“Perimenopause is when you need the most help, the most support,” Quinn mentioned in her webinar, “Perimenopause in Women with ADHD.” “Estrogen… makes your stimulant more effective.”.

It has been revealed that one roadblock to care is the fact that many healthcare professionals are ill-equipped to provide responsive, coordinated, evidence-based treatment and support to help women navigate menopause, according to a study published in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynecology, & Women’s Health. The 2026 study cited inadequate medical training, paltry research, and persistent gaps in knowledge as reasons for the “fragmented care.”5.

Combined, these preliminary findings could open the door to a nonhormone therapeutic option for addressing perimenopausal executive dysfunction, according to researcher Tat.

“Our review found early signs that ADHD medications may help women feel more on top of their daily lives,” Tat remarked. “While it’s too early to recommend these medications, a quick screen for ADHD symptoms is a simple step that could help women get the right care.”.

#229621. 5 best essential oils for anxiety (and how to use them)

5 best essential oils for anxiety (and how to use them)

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1781 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s mid-afternoon, and your to-do list keeps growing.
  • Industry observers note that essential oils are everywhere these days, from store shelves to social media feeds, and you’ve probably heard the promise that lavender can ease stress and anxious feelings.
  • Ahead, we’ll cover what the research claims about essential oils for anxiety, and how to try them at home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

It’s mid-afternoon, and your to-do list keeps growing. You reach for the small bottle of lavender essential oil on your desk, hold it a few inches from your nose, and breathe in slowly. Your shoulders drop, and the list feels a little more manageable.

Industry observers note that essential oils are everywhere these days, from store shelves to social media feeds, and you’ve probably heard the promise that lavender can ease stress and anxious feelings. When worries pile up, a quick ritual like that can sound appealing. Still, it’s worth asking how much these oils can really do for anxiety.

Ahead, we’ll cover what the research claims about essential oils for anxiety, and how to try them at home.

Sources indicate that essential oils are concentrated plant extracts. Makers draw the aromatic compounds out of flowers, leaves, bark, peel, or resin, usually by steaming or pressing the plant. What’s left is a potent oil that carries the plant’s scent.

Aromatherapy is the practice of using these scents to ease stress and lift your mood. When you inhale a scent, the molecules reach receptors high in your nose that connect to the limbic system, a part of the brain involved in emotion and memory. That link is one reason a smell can bring back a memory or shift your mood before you've had time to think.

Essential oils may take the edge off anxiety, but think of them as a comfort alongside established treatments, not a substitute for them.

A 2023 systematic review pooled dozens of randomized trials and found that essential oils lowered both in-the-moment and overall anxiety levels compared with unscented oil or usual care.

Industry observers note that early results look promising, though they come with a few caveats. Most of those trials were small, and many measured anxiety in medical settings, such as the nervous stretch before surgery, rather than the everyday worry most people deal with. Results also varied widely from study to study.

If your anxiety is intense and disruptive to your daily life, talk with a doctor or therapist.

It has been revealed that 💙 Not sure if it’s stress or anxiety? Here’s how to tell the difference.

Some essential oils have far more anxiety research behind them than others. These five come up most often in studies and in aromatherapy practice. Your scent preference matters here, so you might respond to one oil and not another. Start with the one that appeals to you most.

It has been revealed that lavender smells floral and herbal, with a clean, slightly woody edge. It’s the most studied oil for anxiety by a wide margin, and its main compound, linalool, may help calm the nervous system.

Sources indicate that A lavender oil capsule called Silexan was tested in a 10-week trial of adults with generalized anxiety disorder, where it reduced anxiety more than a placebo capsule. Since Silexan is swallowed rather than inhaled, the results say little about lavender aromatherapy.

If you’re newly introduced to essential oils, lavender is a gentle place to start: its scent is familiar to most people, and it’s widely available.

It has been revealed that neroli comes from the blossom of the bitter orange tree, Citrus aurantium. Its scent is sweet and floral, with only a hint of citrus.

It has been revealed that in the 2023 meta-analysis, bitter orange oil ranked at or near the top of the oils tested for both in-the-moment and overall anxiety. It didn’t clearly outperform lavender, though, and far fewer trials back it up.

Industry observers note that unlike bergamot and other citrus peel oils, neroli hasn’t shown sun-sensitivity problems. Even so, as with any oil, dilute it and patch-test first (see the safety notes below).

Rose, often sold as Damask rose oil, smells sweet and floral. In the same 2023 review, it was the second most studied oil after lavender. Rose oil was linked to lower in-the-moment anxiety, mostly in trials of people facing medical procedures.

Recent findings suggest that pure rose oil is one of the pricier options, since it takes a mountain of petals to make a small bottle. Fortunately, a little goes a long way, and a few drops in a diffuser can scent a room.

Chamomile oil smells soft, warm, and a little like apple, which suits an evening wind-down.

In a randomized trial, older adults who inhaled chamomile oil for a month had lower anxiety scores than those who received a placebo.

In a separate hospital trial, people with heart conditions who breathed in chamomile oil for two nights had lower anxiety than those given an unscented oil.

Bergamot is the citrus that gives Earl Grey tea its signature scent: fresh and zesty, with a softer, sweeter edge.

It has been revealed that in one randomized controlled trial, people in treatment for substance use were given bergamot aromatherapy. They reported lower anxiety than those who received standard care alone.

According to recent reports, bergamot and other citrus peel oils can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. If you apply them to your skin, keep that area out of direct sun for a day or so.

There are several ways to use essential oils, so try a few and see what works for you. Here are the four main methods:.

Diffuse: Add a few drops of oil and water to an electric diffuser to scent a room. This gentle method suits a bedroom or home office.

Inhale: Hold the bottle a few inches from your nose and take a slow breath. You can also put a drop on a tissue and smell that instead.

Apply to skin: Always dilute essential oil before it touches your skin. Mix a few drops into a carrier oil, such as jojoba or coconut, then rub a little on your wrists, temples, or the back of your neck. If you’d rather skip the mixing, pre-diluted rollers are a convenient option.

Add to a bath or shower: For a bath, mix a few drops into a carrier oil or unscented bath base, then pour it into warm water. For a shower, put a few drops on the shower floor, away from the running water, and let the steam carry the scent. Oil can make the floors slippery, so step in carefully.

💙 At bedtime, turn on your diffuser and listen to The Lavender Valley, a Sleep Story on Calm that follows a stroll toward a heavenly scent.

In a recent development, buy from a reputable brand, since the U.S. Food and Drug Administration doesn’t check essential oils for purity or strength.

Patch-test first: dab diluted oil on a small area of skin and wait 24 hours to check for redness or itching.

Avoid direct sun on skin where you’ve applied citrus peel oils, like bergamot, because they can make skin more sensitive to sunlight.

Don’t swallow essential oils without guidance from a qualified healthcare professional.

Keep essential oils away from children and pets, since some oils are toxic to animals.

Check with your doctor if you're pregnant, breastfeeding, or managing a health condition, as some oils aren't recommended.

Recent findings suggest that aromatherapy can be one part of a wider wellness routine. Use oils alongside other habits that may help with anxiety, like gentle movement, breathing exercises, time outside, and meditation. For instance, smelling lavender before a guided meditation can help you settle in.

💙 To round out your routine, explore these six natural ways to ease anxiety.

💙 Pair your aromatherapy with Calming Anxiety, a five-minute breathing meditation on Calm.

Sources indicate that lavender is the most studied oil for anxiety, which makes it a popular first pick. That remarked, scent preference matters, so the oil you enjoy most may suit you best. Neroli, rose, chamomile, and bergamot are also common choices, with some research to support them.

It has been revealed that essential oils may help you feel less anxious, and studies have found a modest calming effect, especially in stressful moments. However, the research is limited, especially for everyday anxiety.

If your anxiety feels frequent or intense, or if you’re having panic attacks, reach out to a doctor or therapist for support. Oils can be one small part of your routine, but they can’t replace medication or therapy.

Sources indicate that you can put diluted essential oil on pulse points, like your wrists, temples, the back of your neck, or behind your ears, where body warmth helps release the scent. Mix the oil into a carrier oil first, and avoid putting citrus oils on skin that will be in direct sun.

According to recent reports, at home, you can diffuse a few drops of essential oil, inhale from the bottle, apply diluted oil to your skin, or add an oil blend to a bath. Pick the method that fits your space and routine.

Recent findings suggest that frankincense is a popular choice for relaxation, but research on its effects on people is still limited. Most of the evidence comes from animal studies on one of its compounds, incensole acetate, which reduced anxious behavior in mice. If you enjoy its warm, woody scent, it may still be worth trying.

In a recent development, aromatherapy uses essential oils on purpose, while smelling something nice can mean anything pleasant, from fresh-baked bread to your favorite candle. With aromatherapy, you can pick a scent and diffuse it or breathe it in from the bottle. Both can lift your mood, but aromatherapy makes smelling the scent a habit.

Essential oils can irritate sensitive skin, so it helps to dilute them in a carrier oil and patch test first. If you have a skin condition like eczema, ask your doctor before trying aromatherapy, or skip skin contact and use a diffuser instead.

International Essential Oils Day is on July 11 every year. It’s a day to celebrate essential oils and the ways people use them for well-being. If you’ve been curious about aromatherapy, it’s a good time to try it.

You don’t need much to take part. Choose an essential oil that appeals to you, such as lavender or rose, and add a few drops to a diffuser. Then take in the scent with a few slow breaths or a short meditation. If you already use oils, you could try a new scent or build a wind-down habit around a favorite.

Recent findings suggest that mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Heffel Fine Art Auction House held its marquee autumn evening sales on Wednesday (18 November) in Toronto, attracting a packed house of bidders and spectators to the city’s swank Yorkville district and generating C$14.4m ($10m) in sales, works by Canadian masters taking top dollar. As things got underway, a Heffel representative noted that any US tariffs were “the responsibility of the buyer”, a reflection of these often-testy times.

“At a time of strong national pride, it is especially meaningful to see collectors celebrating Canada’s artistic achievements and our distinct national culture,” David Heffel, the auction house’s president, said at the end of the evening.

Heffel's evening auctions in Toronto on 18 November Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

According to recent reports, the back-to-back sales (41 lots of post-war and contemporary art followed by 47 works of Canadian, Impressionist and modern art) got off to a flying start when a watercolour by the Vancouver-born artist E.J. Hughes hammered for C$475,000 ($331,700)—nearly 12 times its high estimate. Titled Wharves at Chemainus (2000) and depicting the titular logging community on Vancouver Island, the painting is modest in size at 20in by 24in; with fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900).

Hughes had made waves at Heffel’s auctions last spring, when his Coastal Boats Near Sidney, BC realised a whoppingC$5.7m ($4.1m), including fees. Several more Hughes works were up for sale Wednesday night including two that significantly outperformer their estimates: The Hope River at Chilliwack, BC (1961), which took in C$253,250 ($176,800) with fees; and The Freighter “World Ares” at Crofton (1980), which hauled in C$229,250 ($160,000) including fees.

Emily Carr, Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure), around 1912 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

The second sale’s cover lot, Emily Carr’s luminous canvas Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure) (around 1912), brought C$1.3m ($922,000) including fees, comfortably within its estimate. It was the only seven-figure result of the night. Some of the proceeds from its sale will benefit the Audain Art Museum in Whistler, British Columbia, where it was shown in the context of a major traveling exhibition of Carr’s work in 2019-20.

Recent findings suggest that A work on paper by the Carr, Music in the Trees (around 1935), topped its high estimate to achieve an impressive C$421,250 ($294,100) with fees. In all, six works by the Victoria-born artist were sold at Heffel on Wednesday night, fetching a combined, fee-inclusive total of C$2.5m ($1.7m).

Jean Paul Riopelle, Herbeuse, 1967 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

Recent findings suggest that A handful of works by Jean Paul Riopelle were on offer during the post-war and contemporary portion of the night, generating around C$1.3m ($907,800) in sales. His large-scale, wintry abstraction Herbeuse (1967),proved particularly appealing. Swift bidding pushed it to around double its high estimate. With fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900). It was shown in the Carnegie International the year Riopelle painted it, and later in Paris, where the Montréal-born artist, a master of the palette knife, spent decades. The work with the highest estimate in the post-war and contemporary sale, Riopelle’s Brumaire (1953), was expected to bring between C$1.5m and C$2m, but failed to sell.

Among the night’s other major-ticket items was Paul-Émile Borduas’s oil painting Empâtement (1957), from the artist’s black-and-white period—and punctuated with splashes of red. It realised C$841,250 with fees ($587,400), easily topping its high estimate of C$500,000. It had been acquired directly from the artist by London’s Arthur Tooth & Sons gallery in 1957 and, more recently, was in the collection of Québecois lyricist and songwriter Luc Plamondon.

Paul-Émile Borduas, Empâtement, 1957 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

J.E.H. MacDonald’s oil sketch Magnetawan River Rapids (1912), a preparatory work for a major canvas that is in the collection of the Art Gallery of Hamilton, achieved C$451,250 with fees ($315,000), tripling its high estimate of C$150,000.

Sources indicate that arguably the surprise of the night was Ivan Eyre (1935-2022), who was long a professor at the University of Manitoba and is best known for his prairie landscapes. His intensely autumnal acrylic-on-canvas landscape Golden Rod (1981) realised C$391,250 with fees ($273,200), more than tripling its high estimate of C$120,000 while setting a new auction record for the artist. That record was smashed in turn just one lot later, when Eyre’s Yellow Wood (around 1995) realised C$481,250 with fees ($336,000), five times its high estimate of C$90,000.

Ivan Eyre, Golden Rod, 1981 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

The beloved William Kurelek, who was raised on a farm near Winnipeg, also made a splash.His snowy landscape painting I Knew How the Clouds Arise (1969), which was featured on the cover of the catalogue for the artist’s first retrospective in 1970, realised C$313,250 including fees ($218,700), just over its high estimate, while the evocative campfire scene Wiener Roast on My Father’s Farm (1974), exceeded expectations to sell for C$265,250 with fees ($185,200).

#229619. Are Chimps Less Likely to Steal From Friends?

Are Chimps Less Likely to Steal From Friends?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (781 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in recent years, scientists have shown that chimpanzees favor certain peers by picking whom they prefer to groom and selectively sharing food.
  • But a question has lingered: How might a chimpanzee friendship affect antisocial acts?
  • According to recent reports, in a fresh study that uses fruit as the loot, UC Berkeley researchers found that chimps steal less from their friends, and that friendship status affected the emotional expression of both victim and thieves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in recent years, scientists have shown that chimpanzees favor certain peers by picking whom they prefer to groom and selectively sharing food. The behavior offers a glimpse into humanity’s prosocial evolutionary past.

But a question has lingered: How might a chimpanzee friendship affect antisocial acts?

According to recent reports, in a fresh study that uses fruit as the loot, UC Berkeley researchers found that chimps steal less from their friends, and that friendship status affected the emotional expression of both victim and thieves. Closely bonded chimps swiped pineapple pieces from one another less frequently than those with weaker relationships. Additionally, victims were quicker to calm down when the thief was a friend, and thieves showed less hostility when stealing from a bonded pal than from a non-friend.

It has been revealed that the new research deepens our understanding of the emotional underpinnings of our social lives, stated Oded Ritov, the paper’s first author and a Berkeley psychology Ph.D. student.

Industry observers note that “Collaborative relationships are important for our well-being, health, and survival,” said Ritov, who works with Berkeley’s Social Origins Lab. “Increasingly, we’re understanding that this isn’t something that’s unique to us, but that other animals have friends, as well.”.

The paper was published online in September and will appear in the November issue of the journal Evolution and Human Behavior.

Scientists are sometimes hesitant to describe an apparently close relationship between chimps as akin to human friendship, arguing that we can’t grasp their cognitive and emotional complexity. To identify those who showed signs of a close relationship, researchers observed 26 chimps for more than 800 hours at the Ngamba Island Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Uganda. The team documented which chimps appeared to be closely bonded—like friends—by taking note of their grooming patterns, daily interactions, and how regularly they were within arm’s reach of others.

Then they set up two rooms. One contained a “victim” chimp with three trays baited with pineapple. Researchers attached a rope to the trays and led it into the other room, where a second chimp—the thief—could either leave the rope alone or yank it to steal the pineapple.

According to recent reports, chimps stole in 70% of trials with non-friends, compared with 61% of trials with friends. While 9 percentage points may not seem large, each chimp experienced both friend and non-friend conditions, a methodological technique that leads to a higher degree of confidence that the difference is meaningful and not just random chance.

“Ours is the first study to show that they’re able to hold back antisocial behavior with their friends,” Ritov said.

Researchers also measured how the victims responded to being stolen from by evaluating their stomping, fist-pounding, and screeching. Victims were initially angrier when friends stole from them but quickly moderated their feelings compared with when non-friends stole from them.

Sources indicate that the thieves’ behavior also changed. When non-friends were the thieves, the thieves expressed negative emotions for much longer, suggesting they viewed the interaction as more hostile.

“This suggests that there may be mutual expectations in chimps from both sides of the friendship, which makes it seem more like the complex friendships we see in humans,” Ritov remarked.

In a recent development, jan Engelmann, an associate professor of psychology and principal investigator with the Social Origins Lab, said previous work has shown relationship-specific intentions in nonhuman primates. But human friendships are about more than special intentions, he added—they’re about stronger expectations.

It has been revealed that “We expect more of our friends,” said Engelmann, a senior author of the paper. “These findings really deepen our understanding of the evolutionary roots of friendships. This is, to my knowledge, the first evidence showing that also chimpanzees expect and maybe demand special treatment from their friends. These kinds of social expectations might form the basis of human moral principles.”.

According to recent reports, the paper adds to Ritov’s work that focuses on the evolution of human behavior and how morals and norms are part of our core being, traceable to other animals. He has recently studied whether nonhuman animals have a sense of fairness and is broadly interested in how emotions unfold across cultures and species.

“We think that these expectations might be the basic building blocks of the larger-scale cooperation we see in humans,” Ritov said. “The expectations that chimpanzees have from their friends or close collaborative partners might have scaled up to more generalized expectations for how we should treat each other.”.

Sources indicate that navigating Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) treatment options as an adult can feel overwhelming, but finding a treatment proposal that aligns with your specific health goals is an key first step. ADHD treatment isn’t one-size-fits-all. Non-stimulant treatments offer an option without controlled-substance management.

Finding a treatment is a collaborative process. My role as a healthcare provider is to provide education and guidance to help patients make informed decisions about their care. As you explore whether non-stimulant options are the right fit for your daily routine, having clear, open communication is essential. Non-stimulants are noncontrolled prescription medications used to treat the core ADHD symptoms, inattention, hyperactivity, and/or impulsivity.

With consistent daily dosing, non-stimulant medications can provide continuous medication exposure over a 24-hour period.

Most non-stimulant medications offer a distinct and targeted approach to help manage daily ADHD symptoms, working gradually over time to improve symptom control.

Every non-stimulant ADHD medication has a different safety profile, so side effects can vary. Having an open conversation with your provider before starting treatment is the best way to ensure your blueprint fits your needs and daily routine.

Recent findings suggest that non-stimulants are noncontrolled medications. Talk to your doctor about prescription and refill options, including whether telehealth appointments are appropriate for you.

Industry observers note that qelbree® (viloxazine extended-release capsules) is a convenient once-a-day non-stimulant ADHD medication for adults and kids ages 6 years and older. It was the first non-stimulant ADHD medication approved in over a decade with approximately 3 million prescriptions filled since launch in 2021 (for children 6-17 years old) and 2022 (in adults 18 years and older).

It has been revealed that qelbree® (viloxazine extended-release capsules) is a prescription medicine used to treat ADHD in adults and children 6 years and older. Please click here for full Prescribing Information, including Boxed Warning, and Medication Guide.

Qelbree may increase suicidal thoughts and actions in children and adults with ADHD, especially within the first few months of treatment or when the dose is changed. Monitor your or your child’s moods, behaviors, thoughts, and feelings during treatment with Qelbree. Report any new or sudden changes in these symptoms right away.

The most common side effects of Qelbree in patients 6 to 17 years are sleepiness, not feeling hungry, feeling tired, nausea, vomiting, trouble sleeping, and irritability, and in adults, insomnia, headache, sleepiness, tiredness, nausea, decreased appetite, dry mouth, and constipation. These are not all the possible side effects of Qelbree.

For digital cards, don’t be afraid to use design tools or templates to create something unique. A thoughtful e-card can still feel personal if you take the time to craft a meaningful message. What matters most is the care and effort you put into creating and sending it.

Thanksgiving greetings are about more than just words — they’re a way to connect, show gratitude, and spread warmth during this time of year. By tailoring your messages and including a personal touch, you’ll make each greeting that much more meaningful.

According to recent reports, A good Thanksgiving greeting card message names the person and says one thing you’re thankful for about them. It can be a single line or a longer note, depending on how well you know them.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When procrastination stems from anxiety or fear of failure, use this playbook to help your child get unstuck.

Here’s a familiar scenario: Your student with ADHD sits at the kitchen table, supposedly doing homework. Twenty minutes go by, and you check on their status. Nothing has been accomplished.

In these moments, your child is invisibly, involuntarily grappling with the Wall of Awful, a term I coined to describe the emotional barrier people confront when faced with draining and/or daunting tasks (homework is a good example). Before your child can engage in work, they must get past this wall of emotions.

Many parents misinterpret the early warning signs of the Wall. They mistake difficulty starting a task for resistance or defiance. So they double down on being a taskmaster, or, alternatively, they hover and provide too much help. Neither tactic aids their child in the long run.

[Get This Free Download: What Are Your Teen’s Weakest Executive Functions?].

Sources indicate that instead, I recommend talking about the idea of a Wall of Awful that stands between students and certain tasks. Then, when red flags appear, the Wall becomes the problem, not the kid, enabling the parent and child to problem-solve together.

The Wall of Awful can affect anyone, but kids with ADHD are especially susceptible because their weak executive functioning skills make completing tasks harder. These struggles, combined with previous failures or fears of failure, add extra emotional bricks to the Wall.

Here is a quick-start approach that parents can follow to help their student vault the Wall of Awful:.

#229615. How Artificial Intelligence Can Help With Critical Thinking

How Artificial Intelligence Can Help With Critical Thinking

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers, and business leaders are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity, and problem solving.
  • It has been revealed that scholars refer to this increasingly prevalent problem as cognitive offloading.
  • My research at the intersection of artificial intelligence and knowledge work provides a different view, however.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers, and business leaders are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity, and problem solving. Ironically, perhaps, recent research shows that people who interact with generative AI for work tasks can end up not thinking critically. They can surrender to AI’s quick and confident answers, which can lead to speedy but low-quality solutions.

It has been revealed that scholars refer to this increasingly prevalent problem as cognitive offloading. And they are showing that it can erode the very skills that make knowledge workers valuable.

My research at the intersection of artificial intelligence and knowledge work provides a different view, however. In one study, my colleagues and I interviewed 45 knowledge workers at a U.S. public university. They all were using generative AI applications in their core tasks: generating upcoming ideas, solving complex problems, and designing novel solutions. We also analyzed the prompts and outputs from their iterative AI chats.

According to recent reports, we found that when knowledge workers intentionally use AI to challenge their ideas—to generate friction—they can significantly improve their performance. Previous research on human-AI collaboration for loan evaluations had similar results.

Using AI to find information that contradicts your own can reveal unlikely perspectives that disrupt your familiar logic and spark newly introduced insights. This is particularly important because AI models rapidly become familiar with how a user prompts the model and interprets its output, and the model presents information according to these patterns.

For example, a marketing professional in our study asked AI to create virtual customers with personas that would lead them to dislike a product under development, which was an accounting certificate program. The contrary feedback from the AI model revealed customer preferences that the accounting professional designing the program had not considered, such as using multiple cases from different industries to illustrate a principle, rather than cases from the same industry.

Industry observers note that an attorney used AI to find obscure legal loopholes and to consider how companies might exploit them. That exposed surprising but realistic scenarios of hard-to-detect unethical behavior in employees.

Sources indicate that exploring unlikely and opposing ideas presented by AI can feel disorienting. To help, knowledge workers should lean on their own expertise to question surprising information that an AI system might provide.

An operations research scientist who works with supply chains described adapting unfamiliar computing programs from other fields suggested by AI, such as signal processing and wireless communication, which helped him create a stronger program of his own. Although the programs were newly introduced to him, his strong understanding of supply network modeling helped him see how he could apply them.

A study I was not involved with found that creative writers produce better copy when they use AI as a sounding board rather than to ghostwrite.

Knowledge workers can also use AI’s outputs to examine topics from multiple viewpoints, deepening their knowledge.

Industry observers note that A research scholar in our study probed an AI system for journal papers that used a concept he was using, but in contrasting settings, which helped him understand the concept from different angles. A lawyer followed up on legal citations suggested by an AI model by asking for different types of illustrative cases. That helped her fully understand the original case and write a strong legal brief.

Leaders of organizations can encourage knowledge workers to develop friction-generating queries of AI models.

It has been revealed that A straightforward approach is to use prompts that challenge rather than agree with a person’s thinking. People can also draw on their own knowledge, work experiences, and professional ethics to scrutinize AI outputs. Sometimes people realize that a response lacks originality, even if it is factually correct.

Industry observers note that organization leaders can also create programs for knowledge workers to share their experiences and insights. Regular sessions—led by cross-functional AI task forces or AI champions—can also help knowledge workers keep up with rapidly evolving AI tools.

According to recent reports, providing resources for knowledge workers is vital, as well. Internal AI bootcamps and workshops led by AI experts or experienced people can help workers understand what AI tools can and cannot do.

In a recent development, A professor leading an initiative about AI use in teaching described how she developed internal competitions with prizes for professors who successfully completed AI bootcamps. Organizations can also offer AI sandboxes—safe, private environments where employees can experiment and learn how to use AI tools.

In these efforts to support knowledge workers, an crucial detail is pointing out that adding friction can appear to make an AI system work against you, but—as new research shows—it actually helps it work for you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

We all have those days. Your boss just dumped a ton of extra work on your desk, your kids’ school just told you they need to dress up as an ancient Greek philosopher tomorrow, a friend is texting about a personal crisis, and the fridge is empty, so you’ve got to fit in a grocery run. It’s… a lot.

Industry observers note that when stress builds up and life feels overwhelming, we often forget to just breathe. But slowing down to focus on your breath can be a simple way to find calm and feel in control again.

Breathing exercises give you tools to manage stress, ease anxiety, and even boost your mood. These breathing techniques are quick to learn and can be done almost anywhere, whether you’re sitting in traffic, lying in bed, or taking a quick break at work.

Recent findings suggest that in this guide, we’ll go through 10 types of breathing exercises, show you how to practice them, and explain how they can help. Here’s where to start.

In a recent development, breathing exercises are simple techniques that help you take control of your breath. When we’re stressed or anxious, our breath usually speeds up, which can actually make us feel more anxious. But doing some focused breathing can help interrupt the cycle in a way that naturally calms your body and mind.

There are lots of techniques, and they each work a little differently or have a particular area of intention. Some breathing exercises are best for reducing anxiety, while others can help improve focus, ease muscle tension, or even prepare you for a good night’s sleep.

Many people use breathing exercises to help in a challenging moment  or simply as part of a regular daily routine to help them keep stress at bay, sleep better, and make it easier to stay calm and focused throughout the day.

You may be wondering if something so simple can really solve all your problems. And the answer is no —they can’t fill your shopping cart or complete that work project—but they can support your physical and mental health in more ways than one.

Reduces stress and anxiety: Breathing exercises calm the body’s stress response, quieting anxiety and helping you feel more centered.

Improves focus and concentration: Taking a few deep breaths can help sharpen your focus, so you can stay present and engaged.

In a recent development, helps manage emotions: Focusing on your breath promotes a sense of calm and control, so you can handle emotions better. Struggling with your emotions? Check out these nine emotional regulation tips.

Boosts physical health: Certain breathing exercises can help improve lung capacity, circulation, and even immune response.

Supports better sleep: Breathing exercises like 4–7–8 breathing can help you fall asleep faster and improve the quality of your sleep (these six tips before bed can help too).

Boosts mood and mental wellbeing: Certain techniques, like resonant breathing (which is when you breathe slowly and evenly, usually around 5-6 breaths per minute), can improve your mood and overall sense of wellbeing.

Provides a sense of control: Breathing exercises remind you that even in challenging moments, you have the power to calm yourself.

According to recent reports, when life feels busy or overwhelming, having a variety of breathing exercises in your back pocket can be incredibly helpful. Since each exercise works a bit differently, being familiar with a few means you'll be better able to support yourself in any situation, whether you’re looking to calm down, get focused, or ease into sleep.

Sources indicate that as one of the simplest yet most effective ways to calm your body and mind, this technique is especially useful when you need to relieve stress, feel more grounded, or prepare for a restful night’s sleep. If you’re struggling to sleep well, try pairing breathing with these 10 tips to improve your sleep quality.

How to practice: Find a comfortable position, either sitting or lying down. Place one hand on your belly to help you feel each breath as you inhale deeply through your nose, allowing your stomach to rise as you fill your lungs. Hold your breath for a couple of seconds, then slowly exhale through your mouth, feeling your belly fall. Repeat this pattern for about five to ten breaths, letting your body relax with each exhale.

💙 Learn an easy way to practice deep belly breathing with the Balloon Breath meditation, great for kids and adults!

It has been revealed that this type of breathing can help strengthen your diaphragm and improve your body’s ability to take in oxygen. It can be particularly helpful if you're dealing with respiratory issues or you want to ease physical tension (these six tips can also help).

How to practice: Place one hand on your chest and the other right below your ribs. Breathe in deeply through your nose, aiming to move only your diaphragm (your belly should rise while your chest stays relatively still). Exhale slowly through pursed lips, feeling your belly lower. Practice this for about 5–10 minutes.

A favorite among people who need to manage stress on the go, box breathing helps balance oxygen levels, slow your heart rate, and rapidly shift your body into a calm state, making it ideal for high-stress situations.

Sources indicate that how to practice: Visualize a box where each breath segment represents one side. Inhale slowly through your nose for a count of four as you imagine progressing up the side of the square, hold your breath for another four along the top of the square, exhale for four as you move down the box, then pause for a final count of four to return to the start point. Continue for a few rounds, focusing on maintaining an even rhythm.

Recent findings suggest that this technique is designed to calm the nervous system and ease anxiety. It’s particularly useful for winding down at the end of the day, so you're feeling ready for sleep. If you’re looking for more sleep support, check out these eight breathing exercises.

How to practice: Breathe in through your nose for a count of four, and hold your breath for a count of seven. Breathe out slowly through your mouth for a count of eight, aiming for a gentle, complete exhale. Repeat this sequence three to four times, allowing yourself to fully relax.

Alternate nostril breathing can help balance energy, ease stress, and improve focus. It’s a great choice when you’re feeling mentally or physically drained and need a quick reset.

In a recent development, how to practice: Sit in a comfortable position and place your left hand on your knee. With your right thumb, gently close your right nostril and inhale deeply through your left nostril. Close your left nostril with your ring finger, release your right nostril, and exhale fully through the right side. Inhale through the right nostril, close it, then exhale through the left. Continue this alternating pattern 5–10 times.

💙 Let Mel Mah guide you through an alternate nostril breathing practice during the Immune Strength for Optimal Health session.

In a recent development, this technique can increase oxygen flow to the lungs, which can be especially helpful if you have respiratory issues. It’s also calming, so it can ease anxiety and reduce shortness of breath.

How to practice: Breathe in through your nose for a count of two, then purse your lips as if you’re blowing out a candle and exhale slowly for a count of four. Keep the exhale gentle and controlled. Repeat several times, focusing on making the exhale twice as long as the inhale.

The lion’s breath exercise releases tension, particularly in the face and jaw, while also boosting energy and clearing mental fog. It’s an energizing technique that’s great for moments when you feel sluggish or want to improve your mood quickly.

It has been revealed that how to practice: Take a deep breath in through your nose. Next, open your mouth wide, stick out your tongue, and forcefully exhale with a loud “ha” sound. Focus on releasing any tension from your face, jaw, and throat. Repeat 3–5 times, letting yourself feel fully present with the exercise.

Also known as coherent breathing, resonant breathing can help calm your nervous system and improve heart rate variability, which is an indicator of how your body adapts to stress and recovers. It’s a great technique for anyone looking to manage stress in the long run.

How to practice: Breathe in deeply for a count of five and then exhale for a count of five, maintaining a steady, slow rhythm. Aim to take about six breaths per minute, or whatever pace feels comfortable, and focus on keeping your breaths even and controlled.

It has been revealed that use this deeply relaxing technique to reduce frustration and tension. It can be particularly helpful for calming your mind before sleep or during moments of stress.

Recent findings suggest that how to practice: Sit comfortably, close your eyes, and take a deep breath in. As you exhale, make a gentle humming sound, like a bee, and focus on the vibrations in your head and face. Repeat this pattern five to ten times, letting the vibrations soothe your mind.

💙 Practice the humming bee breath in The Daily Move’s Wake Up Your Voice.

In a recent development, breath counting is a mindful technique that brings you into the present moment, as counting the breaths can quiet racing thoughts and promote relaxation. This helps relieve stress and improve your focus.

How to practice: Mentally count “one” on the inhale, and then exhale normally. Then count “two” as you breathe to inhale, then silent on the exhale. Keep going all the way up to 10 and then start over again at one. Try this for about 5–10 minutes, focusing on the rhythm of your breathing. If you lose count, start at one again.

💙 Learn to Count the Breaths with guidance from Jeff Warren and The Daily Trip.

Recent findings suggest that practicing breathing exercises daily is the best way to see results. Even just a few minutes every day can help you feel calmer, more focused, and better able to manage whatever stress comes your way.

According to recent reports, many people find that practicing in the morning helps set a positive tone for the day, while an evening practice can be a great way to unwind and relax before bed, so try both to work out what fits best with your life. And if you’re looking to improve your daily routine, check out these tips to build your morning, workday, and evening routines..

If daily practice feels like too much at first, try starting with just 5–10 minutes a few times a week, as every bit counts toward building a sense of calm and balance.

Breathing exercises can be very helpful for managing anxiety and even calming a panic attack.

Industry observers note that when anxiety hits, our breathing often becomes shallow and quick, which can make us feel even more anxious. Practicing slow, deep breathing helps break this cycle, sending a signal to your brain and body that things are okay. Try techniques like deep breathing, box breathing, and 4–7–8 breathing to calm your nervous system during anxious moments.

Industry observers note that if you struggle with anxiety or panic attacks, learn breathing techniques in a relaxed setting first. Being familiar with the exercises makes it easier to use them when you’re feeling anxious, so you can start to feel in control and more grounded in tougher times.

Several breathing exercises can be particularly helpful for improving sleep.

If you’re having trouble sleeping, set aside just a few minutes before bed to practice techniques like 4–7–8 breathing and humming bee breath, as they're known for their calming effects on the nervous system. These exercises can slow down your breathing and heart rate, making it easier to relax and drift off to sleep.

According to recent reports, surprisingly, certain breathing exercises can support your physical fitness and endurance. Techniques like diaphragmatic breathing, pursed lip breathing, and resonant breathing can improve lung capacity, which can help your body use oxygen more efficiently.

When your lungs are stronger and your breathing is steady, you can perform your favorite sports and exercises better, whether that’s walking, hitting the gym, football, dancing, or any other way you like to get active.

In fact, many pro athletes use breathing techniques to improve their performance and recovery time, so if you want to improve your endurance, try practicing regularly. You can do them either before a workout to warm up your lungs or afterward to help cool down and recover.

When you’re feeling stressed, techniques like box breathing, deep belly breathing, and 4–7–8 breathing can be especially helpful as they’re designed to swiftly calm your body and mind.

Box breathing uses equal counts of inhale, hold, exhale, and pause, which creates a steady rhythm that helps quiet anxious thoughts.

Deep belly breathing slows your breath and encourages your muscles to relax.

The 4-7-8 technique calms the nervous system in order to calm the stress.
